title: Ape and human skull differences form one continuous, roughly logarithmic transformation

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Ape and human skull differences form one continuous, roughly logarithmic transformation

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: The differences between the human skull and the skulls of the chimpanzee and baboon form one continuous integral deformation in which corresponding areas of the grid increase approximately logarithmically downwards and forwards, rather than separate modifications of jaws, braincase and face.

fields.label: Chapter
fields.value: Ch. XVII: On the Theory of Transformations, or the Comparison of Related Forms

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: In both dimensions, as we pass from above downwards and from behind forwards, the corresponding areas of the network are seen to increase in a gradual and approximately logarithmic order in the lower as compared with the higher type of skull; and, in short, it becomes at once manifest that the modifications of jaws, braincase, and the regions between are all portions of one continuous and integral process.

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci On Growth and Form claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: D’Arcy Wentworth Thompson, On Growth and Form (1st ed., Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 1917), Chapter XVII, “On the Theory of Transformations, or the Comparison of Related Forms”; topic “Human and ape skulls”. Scope: skulls of humans and anthropoid primates

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: The taxa, direction and approximate logarithmic relation are quantitatively testable with abundant scans. Standard registration and competing-model evaluation can resolve the geometric claim, though not its developmental interpretation.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Register dense landmarks on human, chimpanzee and baboon skulls, fit one continuous deformation with log-linear area expansion along the stated axes, and compare held-out error with modular craniofacial models.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
A good integral mapping does not prove a single developmental process.

Age, sex and allometry require control.

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: The three skulls are heavily archived as CT and surface scans, and the logarithmic, one-process prediction is a concrete model comparison against modular alternatives. A small team can run that comparison with standard geometric morphometrics. Allometry and landmark scheme are real confounds and do not block a decisive test.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Compare human, chimpanzee and baboon skulls with one continuous transformation and test whether corresponding grid areas increase approximately logarithmically downward and forward. Support would be a single smooth gradient that predicts held-out landmarks; a better fit from separate jaw, face and braincase modules would refute the one-process account.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Size-related allometry can look logarithmic without being a single developmental deformation.

Landmark choice on the face versus the vault changes how continuous the gradient appears.

fields.label: Hypothesis
fields.value: If the differences between the human skull and the chimpanzee (and baboon) skull form one continuous deformation whose grid areas 'increase in a gradual and approximately logarithmic order' from above downwards and from behind forwards, then the local area scale factor of the human-to-ape transformation of the lateral (sagittal) skull profile must be a smooth monotone function of antero-inferior position, with its logarithm roughly linear in that position, rather than a patchwork of region-specific changes.

fields.label: Method
fields.value: The deposit holds per-specimen inter-landmark distances, not coordinates, so the pre-registered secondary plan was run. Each specimen's 39 log distances were centred on their mean (log geometric-mean size correction); species means were taken; the log ratio Pan troglodytes / Homo was formed for each distance. Each of the 21 landmarks was assigned to an ordered region of the human skull from its anatomical name (1 neurocranium/vault/cranial base: BR LD AS OPI BA JP APET EAM SP TS KR; 2 orbit/upper face/nasal/zygomatic arch: NA FM ZS ZYGO NSL; 3 maxilla/palate/alveolar: IS PM PNS MT ZI), and each distance scored by the mean of its endpoint ranks. Spearman rho between score and log ratio, medians by region and a bootstrap over specimens (2000 resamples) were computed; Gorilla and Pan paniscus were run as replications that do not enter the verdict.

fields.label: Pass criterion
fields.value: Pre-registered. Primary plan (landmark coordinates available for Homo sapiens and Pan troglodytes): generalised Procrustes superimposition of all specimens; species mean configurations; projection of the means onto the midsagittal plane (midline landmarks as they are, bilateral landmarks averaged across sides) giving a lateral profile with x = antero-posterior and y = supero-inferior axes defined by the Frankfurt-like orientation of the human mean; fit a 2-D thin-plate spline mapping the human mean to the chimpanzee mean and evaluate its Jacobian determinant J (local area ratio chimpanzee/human) at every landmark of the human mean. Define the down-forward coordinate u = (x_forward + y_downward)/sqrt(2) of each landmark. The claim is supported if (a) Spearman rho(u, log J) >= 0.6 with positive sign, (b) the sign of the correlation of log J with x_forward alone and with y_downward alone is positive in both, and (c) an ordinary linear regression of log J on u explains >= 50% of the variance in log J (the 'logarithmic order' of areas, i.e. geometric progression of area ratio with grid position). Secondary plan (only inter-landmark distances available): log of the ratio of chimpanzee to human mean distance, each distance first divided by the geometric mean of all distances in its specimen; assign each distance by the anatomical names of its endpoints to one of three ordered regions (1 neurocranium/vault/occiput, 2 orbit/upper face/nasal, 3 maxilla/palate/mandible/alveolar); supported if Spearman rho(region rank, log ratio) >= 0.6 and region medians increase monotonically 1 < 2 < 3. If the data also contain Gorilla, the same statistics are reported for Gorilla as a replication but do not enter the verdict. Because baboon (Papio) data could not be located, confidence attached to any verdict is capped at 0.6.

fields.label: Fail criterion
fields.value: Pre-registered. Refuted if Spearman rho(u, log J) < 0.3 (primary plan) or rho(region rank, log ratio) < 0.3 (secondary plan), or if the correlation of log J with x_forward and with y_downward have opposite signs (expansion forwards but contraction downwards or vice versa), or if the regression of log J on u explains < 25% of the variance while log J differs between anatomical regions in a non-monotone way (patchwork rather than gradient). Results between the pass and fail thresholds are 'mixed'. If the deposited file contains neither coordinates nor named inter-landmark distances per specimen (e.g. only summary statistics), the verdict is inconclusive with reason data-unavailable.

fields.label: Unit
fields.value: Spearman rho (region score vs size-corrected log distance ratio Pan troglodytes/Homo)

fields.label: Interpretation
fields.value: Thompson's grids compare lateral profile drawings of one human, one chimpanzee and one baboon skull. His claim has two parts: (1) the human-to-ape change is a single smooth deformation, not independent changes of jaws, braincase and face; (2) within that deformation the local area ratio increases 'in a gradual and approximately logarithmic order' downwards and forwards, i.e. the logarithm of the area ratio grows roughly linearly with position along the down-forward direction. Both are operationalized on species mean landmark configurations via a thin-plate spline (the modern formalisation of Thompson's coordinate transformation): smoothness and single-gradient structure are measured by how much of the variation in log local area ratio is explained by a linear gradient in down-forward position, and the 'logarithmic order' by the sign and strength of that gradient. Searches of Dryad, Zenodo and figshare on 2026-10-31 found no public per-specimen landmark set containing Papio together with Homo and Pan; MorphoSource and Phenome10K scans require a login and would also require digitising landmarks, which is beyond this test. The Zenodo deposit of Schroeder & von Cramon-Taubadel (2017, Evolution) covers 15 extant hominoid taxa including Homo and Pan; its exact contents (coordinates vs distances, per specimen vs summary) were not inspected before this pre-registration, which is why primary and secondary plans are both stated.

fields.label: Datasets
fields.value: Data from: The evolution of hominoid cranial diversity: a quantitative genetic approach (Schroeder & von Cramon-Taubadel 2017, Evolution)

fields.label: Caveats
fields.value:
Secondary (weaker) plan: the deposit gives inter-landmark distances, not landmark coordinates, so no thin-plate-spline area ratios could be computed; distance ratios are linear rather than areal scale factors and position is an ordinal three-level region score assigned by the analyst from landmark names, not a measured coordinate.

No baboon (Papio) data were available; Thompson's statement that the baboon shows 'the same order' of deformation with greater intensity is untested. Gorilla, which Thompson also mentions, shows the same gradient with a steeper slope (0.28 vs 0.22 log units per region step), consistent with his 'increased intensity' remark.

The relation is monotone and roughly linear in log ratio across region ranks (R^2 0.48 for Pan, 0.51 for Gorilla), which is what 'approximately logarithmic order' predicts, but with only three ordinal positions a linear trend cannot be distinguished from other monotone shapes.

Within the neurocranium, cranial-base distances (APET-BA, KR-SP, BA-EAM) have positive log ratios while vault distances (BR-LD, LD-AS, OPI-LD) are strongly negative, in line with Thompson's claim that the gradient runs downwards as well as forwards; this was not a pre-registered test.

Species means of adult crania of mixed sex were compared; the dataset's log distances are size-corrected by geometric mean, so the test concerns shape, whereas Thompson's figures also carried a size difference.

Spearman p-values treat the 39 distances as independent, which they are not (shared endpoints); the bootstrap CI over specimens does not address this dependence either.
